title: Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors
subtitle: Nine strangers inside a sinking ship
summary: Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors is Chunsoft's Nintendo DS visual novel and escape-room adventure, the first game in the Zero Escape series. College student Junpei wakes aboard a sinking liner with eight other abducted people. They are forced into the Nonary Game, where numbered doors and strict rules determine how they can proceed. The immediate task is to escape, but the group also has to decide whom to trust. A closed room becomes one problem inside a larger uncertainty about the people sharing it.
body: Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors is Chunsoft's Nintendo DS visual novel and escape-room adventure, the first game in the Zero Escape series. College student Junpei wakes aboard a sinking liner with eight other abducted people. They are forced into the Nonary Game, where numbered doors and strict rules determine how they can proceed. The immediate task is to escape, but the group also has to decide whom to trust. A closed room becomes one problem inside a larger uncertainty about the people sharing it.

The adventure alternates between narrative passages and Escape sections. In a room, the player examines objects, collects items and works through connected puzzles to find a way onward. Between those practical problems, conversations and decisions shape the route through the ship. The change of pace makes investigation operate on two levels. An object may have a definite use once it is understood, while a person's explanation can remain doubtful. Solving the lock does not settle whether the next decision will place the group in greater danger.

The story branches toward several endings, making the route taken through the ship part of what the player understands about its mystery. Knowledge from an earlier attempt can change how a familiar conversation is read, even before another door has opened. Kotaro Uchikoshi connects the puzzle structure to that accumulating uncertainty rather than treating the rooms as detachable diversions. The handheld's two screens support a game built around reading and acting, giving the same small machine room for an urgent narrative and the close inspection of an apparently ordinary object.
